items.title: int.Parse throws on "abc"; TryParse returns false
items.body:
`int.Parse` expects valid number text. Given "abc" it throws a `FormatException`. The exception lesson shows this: it puts `int.Parse("abc")` inside `try` and catches `FormatException`.

`int.TryParse` never throws for bad text. It returns a `bool` (true if it worked) and puts the number in its `out` variable. Line 52 uses that bool in a ternary: `? parsed : 0`. For "abc" the bool is false, so `safeNumber` becomes 0. The lesson's common mistakes include "Not handling TryParse failures", which is what the ternary handles.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Both return 0": Parse does not return a fallback; it throws.
- "Both throw": TryParse reports failure by returning false, not by throwing, and its out variable is an int, not a message.
- "Parse returns null": an `int` cannot be null; Parse throws instead, and TryParse is the one that does not throw.

excerpts.quote: int number = int.Parse(numberAsText); int safeNumber = int.TryParse("abc", out int parsed) ? parsed : 0;
int x = int.Parse("abc"); } catch (FormatException ex) { Console.WriteLine("Not a valid number: " + ex.Message);

items.title: Core idea: a value copy versus a shared reference
items.body:
Many C# surprises come from one question: when I write `b = a`, do I get a second independent thing, or a second name for the same thing?

- For value types such as `int`, assignment copies the value. Changing `b` afterwards does not touch `a`. The variables bug hunt shows this with `int a = 10; int b = a; b = 99;` and notes that `a` still prints 10.
- For classes, the variable holds a reference (think: an address) to an object. Assigning copies the address, not the object. Both names now point at one object.

Strings are a special case: `string` is a class, but strings are immutable. No string method changes the text it is called on; methods like `Trim` or `ToLower` hand back a brand new string, and if you do not store it, it is lost. The strings think-predict prints `s` again after `s.Trim().ToLower()` to make you check this.

Keep this picture in mind for the classes, strings and records quizzes.

excerpts.quote: int a = 10; int b = a; b = 99; Console.WriteLine(a); // 10
structs value copied, classes reference shared.
Console.WriteLine(s.Trim().ToLower()); Console.WriteLine(s); // predict immutability

The ignored-result string bug and the null string crash.

items.title: Why a.Name prints "new" after changing b.Name
items.body:
`Snack` is a class, so `Snack a` holds a reference to an object, not the object itself. `Snack b = a;` copies that reference. Now `a` and `b` point to the same single Snack. Setting `b.Name = "new"` changes that one object, so `a.Name` prints `new`. The bug hunt's comment says "both changed".

`int` is a value type. `int b = a;` copies the number itself, so `b = 99` changes only `b`; the variables bug hunt prints `a` as 10. Its summary line: structs value copied, classes reference shared.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "old, Name is a field so not shared": being a field does not matter; there is only one object, so there is only one Name.
- "old, class assignment copies the object": that is how value types behave, not classes.
- "does not compile": assigning one class variable to another is ordinary C#; no `new` is needed.

excerpts.quote: Snack a = new() { Name = "old" }; Snack b = a; b.Name = "new"; Console.WriteLine(a.Name); // both changed
int a = 10; int b = a; b = 99; Console.WriteLine(a); // 10

items.title: Why two 1-second tasks with WhenAll take about 1 second
items.body:
`GetDataAsync` is an `async` method. When you call it, it starts running right away, reaches `await Task.Delay(1000)`, and hands back a `Task` that is already in progress. So `var task1 = GetDataAsync();` starts the first delay, and the next line starts the second one a moment later. Both one-second waits run at the same time.

`await Task.WhenAll(task1, task2);` does not launch anything; it waits until both tasks are done. Because the delays overlap, the whole block takes about one second, not two. The lesson describes WhenAll as the tool for running multiple async operations at the same time, and its mini challenge asks for exactly this: two slow operations in parallel.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Nothing starts until WhenAll": the tasks were started by the calls on the two `var` lines.
- "task2 waits for task1": nothing awaits task1 before task2 is created, so they overlap.
- "Must call Start()": tasks returned by async methods are already running; Start() is not needed.

excerpts.quote: public async Task<string> GetDataAsync() { await Task.Delay(1000); // Simulate work return "Data received"; }
var task1 = GetDataAsync(); var task2 = GetDataAsync(); await Task.WhenAll(task1, task2);
Task.WhenAll - Run multiple async operations at the same time

items.title: Start here: how this C# lab is laid out and what to read first
items.body:
This repo is a folder of small C# files, one concept per file, numbered 01 to 19. The README says to follow the numbered files in order and to read each file the same way: the top comment block first, then the code with its comments, then the sections at the bottom (LINE-BY-LINE BREAKDOWN, NOOB TRANSLATION, COMMON MISTAKES).

Many topics also have extra files with the same number:

- `-think-predict.cs`: a tiny program. Before you run it, write down what you think it prints.
- `-bug-hunt.cs`: a short list of real mistakes on that topic.
- `-narrative.cs`: the same idea told as a story about building a SnackTrack console app.

A good reading order for this pack's quizzes:

1. `03-numbers-and-math-operations.cs` (number types, division, parsing).
2. The `02-strings-and-text` lesson, then its think-predict and bug-hunt.
3. `09-classes-and-objects-bug-hunt.cs` and `01-variables-and-data-types-bug-hunt.cs` (copies vs shared objects).
4. The `10-inheritance` and `11-exception-handling` files.
5. `12-async-await.cs`, `13-linq.cs`, `15-records.cs`, `16-delegates-events.cs`, `17-nullability.cs`, each with its bug-hunt if there is one.

To try code, the README suggests a console project, .NET Fiddle or VS Code.

excerpts.quote: 1. Open one file at a time. 2. Read the top comment block. 3. Read code + comments. 4. Use the bottom sections for deeper understanding.
`XX-...-think-predict.cs` — Predict outputs and behavior. - `XX-...-bug-hunt.cs` — Find/fix bugs.

items.title: Why .Result and .Wait() can freeze your program
items.body:
`await` waits without blocking the thread: the thread is free to do other work, and the rest of the method continues later. `.Result` and `.Wait()` do the opposite. They block the current thread until the task is done.

The danger: in some apps the rest of the awaited method (its continuation) needs to run on that very thread. The thread is stuck waiting for the task, and the task is waiting for the thread. Neither can move, so both wait forever. That is a deadlock, which is what both files warn about: the lesson says .Result or .Wait() "can cause deadlocks", and the bug hunt says "blocking on .Result or .Wait() causing deadlock". The cure is to use `await` all the way up.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Turns the caller into async void": async void is a separate bug in the bug hunt's list, not what .Result does.
- "Cancels after 30 seconds": nothing in the lesson mentions a default timeout; blocking waits as long as it takes.
- "Returns before it finishes": blocking is exactly the opposite; it waits for completion.

excerpts.quote: 1. Forgetting await (fire and forget). 2. Using .Result or .Wait() (can cause deadlocks).
// async void (fire and forget + hard exceptions) // blocking on .Result or .Wait() causing deadlock

readMore.why: The async lesson retold as part of the SnackTrack story.

items.title: Why prices use decimal and not double
items.body:
`double` stores numbers in binary (base 2). Many simple base-10 fractions, like 0.1 or 0.01, have no exact binary form, so a double holds a very close approximation. Over many additions those tiny errors can show up as lost or extra pennies.

`decimal` stores numbers in base 10, so a value like 99.99 or 0.01 is kept exactly. The lesson labels the two types plainly: double is "not for money", decimal is "use for money", and its noob translation calls decimal "exact money (never lose pennies!)". "Using double for money" is one of its listed common mistakes.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "double cannot store more than two decimals": double stores many digits (`3.14159` in the lesson); the problem is exactness, not digit count.
- "decimal is faster": the lesson never says that, and speed is not why decimal is chosen; exactness is.
- "the m suffix rounds to two places": the lesson says the `m` suffix is simply required for decimal literals; it does no rounding.

excerpts.quote: double precise = 3.14159; // Floating point (not for money) decimal money = 99.99m;   // Precise decimal (use for money)
decimal money = 99.99m - The 'm' suffix is required for decimal literals
- double: approximate measurements - decimal: exact money (never lose pennies!)

items.title: Why the query prints 60,40 after nums[1] changes
items.body:
The line `var evens = nums.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).Select(n => n * 10);` does not compute anything yet. It only stores the recipe. The LINQ lesson calls this deferred execution: the query runs when you materialize or enumerate it.

`string.Join` is what walks through `evens`, so the query runs at that moment, against the array as it is then. After `nums[1] = 6;` the array is `{1, 6, 3, 4}`. The even numbers are 6 and 4; times 10 gives 60 and 40. Output: `60,40`.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "20,60,40": the query keeps no earlier results to append to; it runs fresh once.
- "20,40": that would be true only if assigning `evens` ran the query; assignment just stores the recipe. Calling `ToList()` there would have captured 20,40.
- "InvalidOperationException": changing an array element before enumeration starts is fine; nothing was being enumerated yet.

excerpts.quote: var nums = new[] {1,2,3,4}; var evens = nums.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).Select(n => n * 10); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", evens));
The query doesn't run until you materialize it (ToList, ToArray, foreach, etc.)

readMore.why: LINQ explained through the SnackTrack story.

items.title: Why Count() then foreach runs the database query twice
items.body:
An `IEnumerable` of orders built from a database query is a deferred query: a recipe, not a list of rows. Every time something walks through it, the recipe runs again. `.Count()` walks it once (one trip to the database), and the `foreach` walks it again (a second trip). The bug hunt names this exactly: multiple enumeration, where db queries run multiple times.

The fix, from the next bug-hunt line: call `ToList()` once. That runs the query a single time and stores the rows in memory; `Count` and the loop then both read that list.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "foreach skips items Count read": each enumeration starts fresh from the beginning; it does not share a position.
- "Count caches the results": it does not; caching is what `ToList()` gives you.
- "can only be enumerated once": a deferred query can be enumerated again; the problem is that it re-runs each time, not that it throws.

excerpts.quote: // Multiple enumeration of IEnumerable (side effects or db queries run multiple times) // Forgetting ToList() when you need to iterate twice
1. Multiple enumeration of the same query. 2. Forgetting ToList() when you need the results now.

readMore.why: More LINQ operators once the basics are clear.

items.title: Why p1 == p3 is True for records with the same values
items.body:
For a `record`, the compiler writes `Equals`, `GetHashCode` and the equality checks for you. The lesson lists this: the compiler generates constructor, properties, Equals, GetHashCode, ToString. Record equality compares the values of the properties, not memory addresses. This is the "value equality" item in the lesson's concept list.

`p1` is Alex Rivera, 28. `p2` is a copy with Age 29, which is why the lesson prints `p1 == p2` as False ("different age"). `p3` is a copy of p2 with Age set back to 28, so p3 holds Alex, Rivera, 28: the same values as p1. Same values means `p1 == p3` is True, even though p3 is a separate object.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Remembers it came from p2": a `with` copy is just a new record with values; it stores no history.
- "== compares references": that is the default for ordinary classes, not for records.
- "== is not defined for records": the lesson itself uses `p1 == p2`.

excerpts.quote: var p1 = new Person("Alex", "Rivera", 28); var p2 = p1 with { Age = 29 }; // Creates new record with change Console.WriteLine(p1 == p2); // False (different age)
- Compiler generates constructor, properties, Equals, GetHashCode, ToString with { Age = 29 } - Non-destructive mutation — creates a copy with changes

items.title: The ! operator silences a warning but changes nothing
items.body:
With nullable reference types on, `string? name` tells the compiler "this may be null". If you then assign it to a plain `string`, the compiler warns you. Writing `name!` is the null-forgiving operator. The lesson's comment reads it as "I promise it's not null". It only tells the compiler to stop warning. It adds no check and no conversion at run time.

In the lesson, `name` really is null (line 18). So `definitelyNotNull` is also null, and reading `definitelyNotNull.Length` throws a NullReferenceException. The lesson lists "Using ! too much (defeating the purpose)" as a common mistake for this reason.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Adds a runtime check and default": that is what `??` does (`name ?? "Unknown"`), not `!`.
- "Throws on the ! line": `!` does nothing at run time, so the assignment itself succeeds; the crash comes when you use the null.
- "Converts to an empty string": no conversion happens; `name?.Length ?? 0` is how the lesson gets 0 safely.

excerpts.quote: string? name = null;           // Can be null
string display = name ?? "Unknown"; int length = name?.Length ?? 0;
string definitelyNotNull = name!; // I promise it's not null
1. Using ! too much (defeating the purpose).

items.title: Core idea: when code actually runs (LINQ queries and async tasks)
items.body:
Two lessons in this lab are about timing: the line where you write something is not always the moment the work happens.

**LINQ deferred execution.** A chain like `nums.Where(...).Select(...)` builds a recipe for a query. The lesson says the query does not run until you materialize it, for example with `ToList`, `ToArray` or a `foreach`. Each time something walks through the recipe, it runs again. That is why the bug hunt lists multiple enumeration as a bug, especially when the source is a database.

**async and await.** An `async` method returns a `Task`, an object that stands for work that will finish later. `await` means "wait here without blocking the thread". The lesson's common mistakes list forgetting `await` and calling `.Result` or `.Wait()`.

When you read the async and LINQ think-predict files, ask for each line: is this line doing the work, or only describing it?

excerpts.quote: Deferred execution - The query doesn't run until you materialize it (ToList, ToArray, foreach, etc.)
await - "Wait here without blocking the thread until this is done"
// Multiple enumeration of IEnumerable (side effects or db queries run multiple times)

Three async mistakes in three lines.

items.title: Why s.ToUpper() alone leaves s as "test"
items.body:
C# strings are immutable: once made, their characters never change. `ToUpper()` builds a new string "TEST" and returns it. The bug hunt calls it on its own line with the comment `// result ignored`, so that new string is thrown away and `s` still points at "test". The program prints `test`. The fix is to keep the result: `s = s.ToUpper();`.

The strings think-predict checks the same idea: after printing `s.Trim().ToLower()`, it prints `s` again, and the original spacing and capitals are still there.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Compile error": C# lets you ignore a return value; that is why this bug is easy to write.
- "An empty line": the method does not clear or move the original text; it never touches it.
- "TEST, changed in place": that would need mutable strings, which C# strings are not.

excerpts.quote: string s = "test"; s.ToUpper(); // result ignored Console.WriteLine(s);
Console.WriteLine("C# strings immutable + watch nulls");
Console.WriteLine(s.Trim().ToLower()); Console.WriteLine(s); // predict immutability

items.title: Why 10 / 3 prints 3 and how to get 3.333
items.body:
`a` and `b` are both `int`. When both sides of `/` are integers, C# does integer division: it keeps the whole-number part and throws away the rest. The lesson's comment marks it as integer division, and its breakdown says it "truncates decimal", so 10 / 3 = 3, not 3.333.

The fix shown in the lesson is to cast one operand first: `(double)a / b`. Now one side is a double, so the division is done in floating point and gives 3.333... (The leftover 1 is what `a % b` returns.)

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "3.33": C# never rounds division to two places; the lesson uses `Math.Round(result, 2)` separately to get 3.33.
- "4": integer division truncates, it does not round to nearest.
- "3.3333333333333335": `/` does not promote to double by itself; you need the cast.

excerpts.quote: Console.WriteLine(a / b);  // 3  ← integer division! Console.WriteLine(a % b);  // 1  ← remainder
double result = (double)a / b;           // 3.333... double rounded = Math.Round(result, 2);  // 3.33
- Performs integer division (truncates decimal) - 10 / 3 = 3, not 3.333

items.title: Why outside code cannot call button.Clicked(...)
items.body:
`Clicked` is declared with the `event` keyword. An event is a delegate with extra rules. The lesson says an event "can only be invoked from inside the class" and that events are delegates with extra safety "so only the owner can raise them". Inside `Button`, `SimulateClick` raises it with `Clicked?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty)`.

Code outside `Button` that writes `button.Clicked(button, EventArgs.Empty);` breaks that rule, so it does not compile. What outsiders may do is subscribe and unsubscribe, with `+=` and `-=`. The lesson's try-changing list says "Subscribe to the Clicked event".

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Compiles if written Clicked?.Invoke": the `?.` only guards against null; the outside-the-class rule still applies.
- "Compiles because it is public": `public` on an event lets others subscribe, not raise it.
- "Compiles but throws": this is a compile-time rule, so it never gets to run.

excerpts.quote: public event EventHandler? Clicked; public void SimulateClick() { Clicked?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
event EventHandler - Special delegate that can only be invoked from inside the class
Events are delegates with extra safety so only the owner can raise them.

items.title: Why the output is "bad format" then "always"
items.body:
Walk the think-predict block in order. Inside `try`, `int.Parse("abc")` throws a `FormatException`. C# looks for a matching `catch`, finds `catch (FormatException)`, and runs it: "bad format" is printed. After try and catch are finished, the `finally` block runs: "always" is printed. The exception was handled, so the program carries on normally.

The main exception lesson describes the same roles: catch is "if it fails, do this instead" and finally is "do this no matter what".

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Only always": finally runs in addition to catch, it does not replace it.
- "always, then bad format": the matching catch runs first; finally runs at the end of the whole statement.
- "always, then a crash": the catch matched the exception type, so nothing is left unhandled, and finally does not rethrow anything.

excerpts.quote: try { int.Parse("abc"); } catch (FormatException) { Console.WriteLine("bad format"); } finally { Console.WriteLine("always"); }
try = "attempt this" catch = "if it fails, do this instead" finally = "do this no matter what"

readMore.why: Common exception-handling mistakes, such as catching too broadly.

items.title: Why new prints "..." when the variable is typed Animal
items.body:
In the think-predict, `Animal.Speak` is `virtual` and `Dog` uses `override`. With `override`, the call `a.Speak()` looks at the real object (a Dog) and prints Woof. That is polymorphism.

If Dog wrote `public new void Speak()` instead, Dog would get a second, unrelated method that only hides Animal's one. Which one runs then depends on the variable's declared type. `a` is declared as `Animal`, so the call runs Animal's version and prints "...". The bug hunt warns exactly about this: forgetting `override` gives hiding, not polymorphism.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Woof, whatever the keyword": only `override` makes the call follow the actual object; `new` does not.
- "Woof twice": neither keyword chains the base and derived bodies; one method runs.
- "Does not compile": `new` is a legal way to redeclare a member; the bug hunt calls the difference subtle, not an error.

excerpts.quote: class Animal { public virtual void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("..."); } class Dog : Animal { public override void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("Woof"); }
// Forgetting override keyword leads to hiding instead of polymorphism // new vs override difference is subtle and catches many devs

readMore.why: The main inheritance lesson with virtual and override.
